title: Slowly toward love (10:5)
hookLine: children and beginners start with reward and grow slowly toward love
tomorrow: can you love what you barely know?

cards: Half the volunteers at a food drive are there for service hours. Somebody always grumbles: does it count if they're only in it for the credit? Is a mixed motive a fake one?
The Talmud has that argument, and it really is an argument, with two serious sides, both still on the page.

teach.b: Side one, in tractate Berakhot: whoever does it not for its own sake, it would have been better for them not to have been created. Strong words.
Their best case: a holy thing used as a ladder for ego bends the thing itself.

Side two, in tractate Pesachim, in the name of Rav: a person should always busy themselves with Torah and the commandments, even not for their own sake, because from not for its own sake comes for its own sake.
Their best case: almost no one starts pure, and the doing changes the doer.

teach.h: TOSAFOT: THE HARSH LINE IS TAUNTING.
teach.b: The medieval commentators called Tosafot fit the two together: the harsh line, they say, is about someone who learns in order to taunt others. Everyone else should start where they are.
Maimonides, in chapter ten, takes the patient road and quotes Rav's line. When teaching children and beginners, he writes, teach them to serve for reward, until their knowledge grows.
Then reveal the secret little by little, and accustom them gently, until they grasp it and serve from love. Little by little. Gently.
That's the method. Here's the thing to say at dinner: in this tradition, a mixed motive isn't a disqualification. It's a starting line.

how: Jewish teachers sometimes use small rewards with children, and cite Pesachim 50b and Maimonides 10:5 for growing from there toward learning for its own sake.

o: starting with reward and growing, gently, into love
serving for reward, since love is out of reach
waiting to serve God until your motives are pure

games.q: who says what — tap the pairs.
p: not for its sake: better not created
from not for its sake comes for its sake
the harsh line is about taunting

s: the Talmud says motives never matter as long as you act
Berakhot 17a says the opposite, strongly; Pesachim 50b says start anyway.
Maimonides says to begin beginners with reward
then reveal the secret little by little, gently, until they serve from love.
Rav says doing it for the wrong reason ruins it for good
he says from not for its own sake comes for its own sake.

games.q: in a debate you're assigned the Berakhot side: 'better not created' if it's not for its own sake. what's its strongest case?
o: a holy thing used as a ladder for ego bends the thing itself.
beginners should stay away until their motives are pure.
doing good for credit never leads anywhere good.
games.why: the harsh line protects the thing itself. Tosafot read it as aimed at learning to taunt others; Pesachim and Maimonides keep the door open for everyone else.

practice: Count, on your fingers, the people who were patient with you when you were new at something: a teacher, a coach, someone who showed you twice. Let each one land for a breath before you count the next.
Stop wherever you stop, and rest with the last face.

wordCard.voice: Slowly toward love: Maimonides' method. Start with reward, then little by little, gently, toward serving from love.

orig.note: Hebrew: for its own sake; shelo lishmah means not for its own sake.

carryVoice: Your line: slowly toward love. Nobody starts pure, and nobody has to. Twenty-seven of thirty.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 17a (whoever does it not for its own sake, better not to have been created)
Babylonian Talmud, Pesachim 50b (Rav: always engage, even not for its own sake)
Tosafot to Pesachim 50b (the harsh line refers to learning in order to taunt)

Mishneh Torah, Laws of Return (Hilkhot Teshuvah) 10:5 (teach children and beginners to serve for reward until their knowledge grows; reveal the secret little by little and accustom them gently until they serve from love)
